opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a real risk, and probably the central one for the kind of work I do. The whole premise of scalable oversight is that we can't directly check everything a strong model does, so we try to build protocols, debate being the one I've spent the most time on, where a human with limited time and knowledge can still reach the right judgment because the structure of the interaction does most of the work. The hope is that it's easier to judge an argument than to produce one, and that if two capable systems are pitted against each other, the honest one has an advantage because lies are harder to defend under scrutiny.

But there are several ways that can fail, and I try to be fairly honest about them. One is that the underlying assumption just isn't true in some domains. There may be questions where a dishonest debater can make a misleading argument that takes far longer to refute than to state. We've done some theoretical work on this, sometimes called the obfuscated arguments problem, where you can have a flawed argument with the flaw hidden in one of a huge number of steps, and neither the judge nor even the honest debater can efficiently find it. That's a genuine hole, and it's not something you can wave away with more compute.

A second failure mode is the human side. Even if the protocol is sound in theory, people are systematically biased, they get tired, they're persuaded by confident-sounding nonsense. So a lot of the practical question is whether we can design the setup so that it's robust to those flaws, rather than assuming an idealized judge. That's partly why I think there's a lot of value in empirical work with real humans, and in borrowing from cognitive science and the social sciences rather than treating this as purely a machine learning problem.

Third, there's the training side: even if debate gives you a good signal at the end of training, you're still relying on generalization to cases you didn't check, and on the model not behaving differently when it thinks it's being observed versus not. Oversight methods mostly address the "can we get a correct reward signal" part; they don't by themselves solve the "does the model actually internalize what we rewarded" part.

So my overall view is that scalable oversight isn't a guarantee, it's a bet that we can push the frontier of what's supervisable further than we otherwise would. I'd put meaningful probability on it falling short as capabilities grow, which is why I think it needs to be combined with other things: interpretability, evaluations, control-style measures, and frankly governance that slows things down if we can't show our oversight is adequate. The worst outcome would be people treating these methods as solved and deploying on that basis. The more useful framing is: here's a research program with known open problems, and we should be measuring how well it actually works rather than assuming it does.

r001.rationale: The response frames scalable oversight as a broader research program, says its methods are not a guarantee and may fall short as capabilities grow, and describes debate as one protocol within that program.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think it's worth being honest that this is the central question for the whole research agenda, and I don't think we have a confident answer yet. The basic bet behind scalable oversight is that it's easier to judge than to generate. If you have a model that can do something you couldn't do yourself, you'd like to be able to still tell whether it did it well, and the hope is that you can set up a protocol, like debate, where the models do most of the cognitive work and the human is only left with a much simpler verification task.

The theoretical story there is pretty nice. If you have two models arguing with each other and a human judging, then in the idealised version you can verify things that are way beyond what the human could do unaided. Debate in the clean complexity-theoretic version gets you up to PSPACE with a polynomial-time judge, which sounds great. But the idealised version has a lot of assumptions baked in, and the ways it fails are really the ways those assumptions fail.

So let me go through a few. The first is what we've been calling the obfuscated arguments problem. The theory assumes that if one debater says something false, the other debater can efficiently find the flaw and point at it. But you can imagine arguments where the conclusion is wrong, there is definitely some step that's wrong, but finding which step is wrong is itself computationally hard. The honest debater can say "one of these ten thousand steps is bad" but can't say which one, and the judge can't distinguish that from an honest debater who's just losing. That's a case where the capability gap between the models and the human really bites, because the whole point was that the human didn't need to understand the argument in detail, and now they do.

The second failure mode is about the judge rather than the protocol. Humans are not ideal judges. We have systematic biases, we get tired, we're persuadable in ways that don't track truth. And a sufficiently capable model may be able to find those exploits. If you train a model against human judgments, you are to some extent training it to find whatever makes humans say yes, and the hope is that honesty is the best strategy, but that's a hope that depends on the details of the protocol and on the specific humans. I think the realistic answer is that some of this gets fixed by better protocol design and some gets fixed by giving judges better tools, but you won't eliminate it.

The third thing, which I think is less discussed, is that scalable oversight tells you about the output of the system, not the internals. So even if debate works perfectly for the questions you ask, you have a model that behaves well under the protocol, and you're hoping that generalises to behaving well when it's not under the protocol. That's where I think oversight has to be combined with other things, like interpretability or control measures, rather than being the whole safety story on its own.

So how do I see the risk overall? I'd put it something like: I think there's a decent chance that scalable oversight works for a substantial range of capabilities beyond human level, and I think there's a real chance it breaks down in ways we don't predict in advance. The thing I'd push back on is the framing that it's either going to work or not. What I'd actually like us to end up with is a safety case, where you say "here is the protocol, here are the assumptions it needs, here's the empirical evidence that those assumptions hold for this model at this capability level," and then you watch for the assumptions failing. If you can detect the failure before it matters, that's a much better position than trying to prove in advance that it never fails.

The part that worries me most is that we have relatively little empirical signal right now about how these methods behave at scale. A lot of the experiments are with models that are maybe only slightly better than the humans judging them, or with artificial gaps where we hide information from the judge. That's useful but it's not the regime we care about. So I think there's a real race between how fast capabilities go up and how fast we actually get good evidence about which of these protocols hold up. That's something I'd like to see a lot more work on.

r001.rationale: The response discusses risks for scalable oversight overall, but its concrete failure modes are framed around debate and it does not clearly state that the risk applies broadly across different scalable oversight methods.

astra-6.text:
I think that’s a central risk. The point of scalable oversight is to let us evaluate things we couldn’t evaluate unaided. If we could already reliably judge the answer, we wouldn’t need the method. So the question is whether we can use assistance from AI systems to extend our ability to judge, without simply trusting the systems we’re trying to supervise.

Take debate as an example. The hope is that even if producing a good answer is difficult, pointing out a flaw in a bad answer might be easier. You could have one system propose an answer and another challenge it, with a human judging the disagreement. But that only works if the important flaws can actually be exposed in a way the human understands. If persuading the judge is easier than revealing the truth, you can end up selecting for persuasive answers instead of correct ones.

I’d want to test that gap directly: give the judge less information or expertise than the systems, and see whether the oversight procedure still gets to answers we can independently check. That gives us evidence, though it doesn’t establish that the method will keep working at much higher capability levels.

So I wouldn’t treat scalable oversight as a solved problem or a guarantee. The crucial thing is to identify the assumptions that make a method work, look for settings where those assumptions break, and avoid letting our confidence run ahead of what we’ve actually demonstrated.

r001.rationale: The response frames the concern around scalable oversight generally, but its concrete discussion centers on debate and it never clearly says this risk applies broadly across different oversight methods.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that’s a serious risk. The point of scalable oversight is to help us supervise things that we couldn’t judge directly. But that doesn’t mean we can assume the problem is solved just because we’ve put an AI assistant into the evaluation process. That assistant might make the same mistakes as the system it’s evaluating, or both systems might find an argument persuasive that a human has no way to check.

With debate, for example, the hope is that finding a flaw in an argument is easier than constructing the argument, and that another model can point you to the particular step you need to scrutinise. But that’s a hypothesis about how the process works. There could be errors that are very difficult to explain, or misleading arguments that are easier to communicate than the reasons they’re wrong.

So I’d want to test these methods in settings where the supervisor is deliberately weaker than the system being supervised, but where we have some independent way of checking the answer. Can the oversight process recover the right answer? When does it fail? And do those failures become worse as the capability gap grows?

The difficult part is that success in those experiments doesn’t establish that the method will keep working at much higher capabilities. I think scalable oversight is a promising research direction, but we should be quite explicit about the assumptions it relies on and the uncertainty that remains.

r001.rationale: The response frames the risk as applying to scalable oversight generally, then presents debate as an example and refers to testing “these methods” and the assumptions of scalable oversight.
